newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African state claims 800 mln rand of KWV assets.
newsitem.headline: S.African state claims 800 mln rand of KWV assets.

text.p: The South African government claims to own 800 million rand ($170 million) of KWV assets and wants them back before the wine and brandy co-operative converts to a public company, the Cape Town high court was told on Monday.

KWV lawyer Philip Ginsburg told the court the figure had been arrived at by an auditor appointed by Land Affairs and Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom, who is seeking in court to block the co-operative's restructuring.
Among the arguments raised by Hanekom is his contention that KWV obtained at least some of its assets because of its role as statutory regulator of the wine and spirit industry.
He has said those assets belong to the state and should not be distributed among KWV members -- mainly wine farmers -- as part of the co-operative's plan to become a public company.
Ginsburg told the court Hanekom was trying to make out that KWV was an organ of state so he could gain control of its assets.

"That's an attempt to expropriate without compensation," he said. "It is not uncommon for governments to look with envy at successful private enterprises. The government is seeking to enrich itself at the expense of Cape wine farmers."
Ginsburg said the KWV had been set up in 1918 by wine farmers as a way of dealing with periodic surpluses. The co-operative was given excess wine which it stored, turned into brandy, and sold abroad.
The lawyer said the KWV was not an organ of state but a private enterprise, despite having benefited from the provisions of the Wine and Spirit Control Act under which it obtained statutory powers.
He said that to rule that a company which obtained benefits from favourable laws automatically became a debtor of the state would set a dangerous precedent.
The diamond giant De Beers, for example, would be liable to pay the government "trillions of rand" which it had made with the help of laws controlling trade in diamonds, Ginsburg said.
The auditor appointed by Hanekom said in his report that the total value of KWV, which operates in about 50 countries, was 1.8 billion rand.
KWV decided last year to convert to a public company so it would be better placed to expand internationally.
Its executives say the restructuring would allow it, among other things, to sell shares to black business groups seeking to gain footholds in South African industries previously dominated by whites.
Lawyers for Hanekom are due to present their arguments later.
They have asked the judge to postpone any ruling until completion of a separate inquiry by the Competitions Board into the implications of KWV's restructuring.
Ginsburg described the request as cynical and said it amounted to an attempt by Hanekom to circumvent the jurisdiction of the court.
